rejected.title: Sahul and the sea crossing
card: In the last ice age, much of the world's water was frozen in ice sheets, so sea levels were far lower than today.
Low seas exposed land between Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania, joining them into one continent called Sahul.
Asia's coast also reached further out. But deep water between the islands kept Sahul apart from Asia, even when the seas were lowest.
So the first people to reach Sahul had to cross open sea, probably by raft or canoe. That took planning and skill, which shows they were skilled seafarers.
rejected.remember: Low seas made Sahul one land, but people still had to cross open sea to reach it.

a.q: What did low sea levels in the last ice age do?
opts: Joined Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania
Joined Sahul to Asia with a wide land bridge
Split Australia from New Guinea and Tasmania
Covered the coasts of Sahul with deep sea
a.why: Low seas exposed land between Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania, joining them into Sahul. They did not join Sahul to Asia, because deep water still lay between them.

b.q: Stone tools show people reached Sahul tens of thousands of years ago, during the last ice age. What does this tell us about them?
opts: They came by sea, so they had boating skills
They walked from Asia across dry land
They came when the seas were higher than now
They came from New Guinea, which was in Asia
b.why: Sahul was never joined to Asia, so anyone who reached it had to cross open sea, which took planning and skill. Walking across dry land is the tempting mistake: the low seas joined Sahul's parts, but not Sahul and Asia.
b.clue: Was there ever a land path from Asia to Sahul?

version.title: Sahul and the sea crossing
card: In the last ice age, much of the Earth's water was locked up in ice, so sea levels were far lower than today.
Low seas uncovered land between Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania. They were joined into one continent, called Sahul.
Even with the seas at their lowest, stretches of deep, open sea lay between Asia and Sahul. Some gaps were tens of kilometres wide.
So the first people to reach Sahul had to cross open sea, probably on rafts or canoes. That needed planning and skill, so they were skilled seafarers.
version.remember: Sahul was one land, but reaching it from Asia still meant a sea voyage.

a.q: Why was Sahul one continent in the last ice age?
opts: Low seas uncovered land between its parts
High seas covered the gaps between islands
Ice sheets formed a bridge across the sea
A dry land bridge joined it to Asia
a.why: With much of the water locked up in ice, sea levels fell and uncovered land between Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania, joining them. Sahul was never joined to Asia: open sea always lay between them.
a.clue: Where was much of the world's water then?

b.q: A student says the first people of Sahul could have walked all the way from Asia, because sea levels were low. What is wrong with this?
opts: Open sea still lay between Asia and Sahul
Sea levels were higher then than they are now
New Guinea was not part of Sahul back then
Low seas split Australia from New Guinea
b.why: Low seas joined Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania, but deep, open sea still lay between Asia and Sahul. So the first people had to cross by water, which shows they were skilled seafarers.
b.clue: Was there ever a dry path from Asia to Sahul?

a.best: Low seas uncovered land between its parts

b.best: Open sea still lay between Asia and Sahul
